---
title: "The product rule"
---

Suppose a corpus annotation tells us two things that are easy to summarize separately: half of the represented pronouns are plural, and among plural pronouns, eighty percent are accusative. How can we recover the probability that a pronoun is both plural and accusative?

The [definition of conditional probability](conditional-probability.qmd) already contains the answer:

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)}{\mathbb{P}(P)}.
$$

Here $P$ is the plural event and $A$ is the accusative event. Multiply both sides by $\mathbb{P}(P)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P)
=\mathbb{P}(A\cap P).
$$

Writing the joint probability first gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)
=\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P).
$$

This expression is the [**product rule**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html), also called the [**multiplication rule**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). It writes one joint probability as a product of a conditional probability and the probability of its condition.

## Reconstruct the joint probability by hand

The pronoun measure gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(P)=.50
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80.
$$

Substitute these two values into the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)
&=\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P)\\
&=.80\times.50\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}
$$

The multiplication has a direct interpretation. The conditioning event $P$ receives half of the total mass. The event $A$ receives eighty percent of that plural mass. Eighty percent of one half is $.40$.

We can check the same logic with counts. Imagine 100 pronoun tokens.

1. If 50 are plural, then the plural event contains 50 tokens.
2. If 80 percent of those 50 are accusative, then 40 tokens are both plural and accusative.
3. Those 40 tokens make up 40 percent of all 100 tokens.

The product rule is the proportional version of this count calculation.

```{r}
#| eval: false
p_plural <- .50
p_acc_given_plural <- .80

p_plural_and_acc <- p_acc_given_plural * p_plural
p_plural_and_acc
```

The result is `.4`.

## Reverse the order of the factors

An intersection is symmetric:

$$
A\cap P=P\cap A.
$$

We can thus begin from the opposite conditional probability:

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)
=\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A).
$$

In the toy measure,

$$
\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)=\frac{.40}{.70}
$$

and $\mathbb{P}(A)=.70$. The reversed product is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)
&=\frac{.40}{.70}\times.70\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}
$$

The factors differ across the two orders. The product does not. Both products reconstruct the mass in the same intersection.

This gives the identity

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P)
=\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A).
$$

We will use exactly this equality on the next page. No additional probability assumption has been made.

## What the product rule does and does not claim

The product rule is an algebraic rewriting of a joint probability. It does not claim that $A$ and $P$ are unrelated. In fact, the factor $\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)$ explicitly allows the probability of $A$ to depend on the condition $P$.

This point matters in linguistic applications. If a speaker's use of a reduced form depends on whether the word is predictable in context, we can still factor the joint event as

$$
\mathbb{P}(\text{reduced}\cap\text{predictable})
=\mathbb{P}(\text{reduced}\mid\text{predictable})
 \mathbb{P}(\text{predictable}).
$$

The product rule represents the dependence through the conditional term.

## A product does not imply independence

A product representation does not by itself imply independence. The presence of a multiplication sign does not justify replacing

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
$$

with

$$
\mathbb{P}(A).
$$

That replacement is a separate claim about independence, which has not yet been established. The product rule itself holds whenever the conditional probability is defined.

## Check your understanding

1. Starting from the definition of $\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)$, derive $\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)=\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)$.
2. Suppose $\mathbb{P}(P)=.30$ and $\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.60$. Compute $\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)$ and interpret the result among 100 tokens.
3. Explain why the two orders of the product rule have different factors but the same product.
4. Which unjustified substitution treats the two chain rule factors as independent?

The two orders reconstruct the same intersection. On the [next page](bayes-rule.qmd), we equate those products and solve for a reversed conditional probability.
